summary: Early (ages 5–7) informal vocabulary-building for the three states of matter — solid, liquid, gas — anchored to OBSERVABLE BEHAVIOUR rather than abstract definitions: a solid keeps its shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container (forms a pool not a pile), a gas spreads out to fill whatever holds it. Water is the through-line (ice, water, steam) so one familiar material carries all three words plus 'change of state'. It deliberately makes an invisible gas tangible (air in a balloon) to begin unseating 'gas is not stuff'. This seeds the later UK Year 4 objective; at this age there is no KS1 statutory states content, and NGSS has no performance expectation dedicated to naming the three states. (Steam, meaning water vapour, is the gas state and is invisible; the white cloud seen above a kettle is tiny drops of liquid water that form as the steam cools, so it should not be presented as the gas.)
misconceptions: Gases are not matter / are weightless — rooted in 'seeing is believing' since most gases are invisible (a very common and persistent idea).
A 'solid' must be hard and rigid, so powders and sand (which pour) get miscalled liquids.
Thinking of a liquid as anything that pours, conflating flow with the liquid state.
The everyday meaning of 'gas' (fuel) crowding out the physical-state meaning.
Treating steam/water vapour as something other than water, or as 'hot air', rather than water in its gas state.

activities.title: Tap-to-name the three states in a kitchen scene
steps: Explore a home/kitchen scene and tap everyday items to hear each one's state and the behaviour reason, e.g. tap the ice cube → 'SOLID — it keeps its shape'; tap the juice → 'LIQUID — it flows and takes the shape of the cup'; tap the kettle → 'When water boils it becomes steam, a GAS you can't see — it spreads out into the air. The white cloud is tiny water drops made as the steam cools.'

Visit a dedicated water trio panel showing the SAME water as hard ice, runny liquid, and invisible steam (water vapour) shown as spreading arrows or a dotted cue, with audio explaining that you can't see the gas itself.
Open a 'melting' and a 'boiling' flap on the water panel to hear that the move between states is called a 'change of state'.
Tap the balloon in the corner to hear 'the air inside is a GAS — it fills the balloon up'.
activities.insight: Three new category words attach to familiar things through how they behave (shape and container), and the SAME water can be solid, liquid or gas (the gas, steam or water vapour, is invisible), with 'change of state' naming the move between them; a gas (air) really is stuff that spreads out to fill its container.

activities.title: Sort real substances into solid / liquid / gas bins
steps: Drag or place plentiful everyday substances into three bins labelled solid, liquid and gas.

For a chosen item, trigger a short 'watch it behave' action — a liquid pouring and taking the shape of a cup, a solid holding its shape, a gas (shown with a coloured animation cue, since most gases are invisible) spreading to fill a jar — and check the sort against the behaviour.
Discuss borderline cases out loud: Is sand a solid when it 'pours'? What about honey, sugar, salt, or a damp sponge?
Use a mini melt/boil before-after pair to practise the words 'change of state'.
activities.insight: The defining test is BEHAVIOUR (keeps its shape / flows and takes its container's shape / spreads to fill the space), not surface looks, size, smell or wetness; tricky cases like pourable powders are still solids because each grain keeps its shape.

activities.title: Use the words like a scientist (checkpoint)
steps: Name whether each of several things is solid, liquid or gas AND describe HOW it behaves: a rock, milk, the air in a balloon, and sand.
Explain what 'change of state' means, using ice as the example (ice melting to water, or water freezing back), including what happens to ice on a warm day.

Answer probing questions: Is the air in the balloon solid, liquid or gas — how can you tell it's really there? Sand pours like a drink — is sand a liquid? Look closely at one grain. Is toothpaste a solid or a liquid — what makes it hard to decide?
activities.insight: Correct, meaningful USE of the behaviour-vocabulary in context (including tricky cases) shows genuine understanding, not recitation of the three words.

checkQuestion: Say: 'I'll name some things and I want you to tell me, like a scientist, whether each is a solid, a liquid or a gas — and describe HOW it behaves using proper words: a rock, milk, the air in a balloon, and sand.' Then: 'Now tell me what “change of state” means, using ice as your example.' Listen for the words used correctly, not recited.
checkAnswer: Rock = solid (hard, keeps its shape); milk = liquid (runny, flows, takes the shape of its container); the air = gas (spreads out, fills the balloon); sand = tiny solid grains (each grain keeps its shape, though the pile pours). 'Change of state' = when ice (solid) melts to water (liquid) on heating, or water freezes back — the same material in a different state.
